pair_interpretation: A pair is meaningfully distinct when its alternatives assert different values or different event classifications; notes separately identify options with weak diagnostic explanations.

items.answer_justification: Each roll has three even faces out of six; two independent rolls give (3/6)^2 = 1/4.
items.topic_fit: Probability of two even outcomes on repeated die rolls.
items.assumptions: Separate rolls of a fair die are treated as independent; this is the ordinary reading of “rolled twice.”

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must identify 2, 4, and 6 as even die faces, then combine the two roll probabilities.

weak_distractors: B (2/3) has no clear route from the three even faces.
D (1/3) has no clear two-roll calculation.
items.answer_cues: No visible position or wording cue; the correct value is not uniquely styled.

items.answer_justification: Expected gross prize is (1×$150 + 2×$25)/200 = $1.00; subtracting the $2 ticket price gives -$1.00. None of A–D matches.
items.topic_fit: Expected value with unequal prize outcomes and a ticket cost.
items.assumptions: Each of the 200 tickets is equally likely to be the one purchased; the prize categories are disjoint.

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must use the counts and payouts for all prize categories and the $2 purchase cost to form the net payoff.

weak_distractors: All four choices are wrong; B (-$1.50) and C (-$0.50) lack an obvious calculation.
A ($0.75) is the gross contribution of the $150 prize alone; D (-$1.25) subtracts ticket cost from that contribution while omitting the two $25 prizes.
items.answer_cues: The missing -$1.00 answer makes the item unanswerable; positive A might cue a failure to subtract cost, but no choice is valid.

choice_pairs.assessment: A is a positive gross component while B is a negative net figure; neither equals the full expected net.
A is positive and C negative; both differ from the actual -$1.00.
A can reflect only the top-prize gross contribution; D can reflect subtracting cost from that incomplete contribution.
B and C are distinct negative values, though neither maps clearly to the stated full calculation.
B differs from D; D has a plausible omitted-consolation-prizes route, B does not.
C differs from D; D has a plausible incomplete-payout route, C does not.

items.answer_justification: There are 4 + 3 = 7 non-green marbles among 4 + 3 + 5 = 12 total, so P(not green) = 7/12.
items.topic_fit: Single-draw probability and a complement expressed through category counts.
items.assumptions: The marble is uniformly drawn from the bag, as “at random” implies.

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must combine the red and blue counts, or count five green out of twelve and complement that derived probability. No probability is supplied directly.

weak_distractors: C (5/7) compares green to non-green counts rather than an event count to the total.
items.answer_cues: The capitalized NOT emphasizes the complement but does not disclose the answer; D has no special formatting.

choice_pairs.assessment: 5/12 is green; 1/3 is red only.
5/12 uses green over all marbles; 5/7 uses green relative to non-green marbles.
5/12 is green; 7/12 is not green.
1/3 is red only; 5/7 compares green with non-green counts.
1/3 includes red only; 7/12 includes red and blue.
5/7 uses the wrong denominator and event; 7/12 uses non-green over all marbles.

items.answer_justification: A single spin cannot land on red and blue at once, so the events are mutually exclusive; four of five sectors are red or blue.
items.topic_fit: Mutually exclusive events and their union on one spinner.
items.assumptions: One spin lands on exactly one of five equal sectors.

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must use the one-spin red/blue sector separation to classify the events, and count the four favorable sectors.

weak_distractors: D (not mutually exclusive; 2/25) combines a wrong relation with a product that lacks a clear route from the stated sector probabilities.
items.answer_cues: A and B share 4/5, so the event-relation decision cannot be bypassed by spotting the correct fraction.

choice_pairs.assessment: The same 4/5 union probability is paired with opposite exclusivity judgments.
A and C differ on exclusivity and on whether the union is 4/5 or 2/5.
Both deny exclusivity but give different union probabilities.
Both classify the events as exclusive; B counts red plus blue while C counts only two sectors.
B and D differ on both event relation and union probability.
C and D differ on both event relation and union probability.

items.answer_justification: Given the first selected student was a boy, 9 boys remain among 24 students, so the second-boy probability is 9/24.
items.topic_fit: Conditional probability for sampling without replacement.
items.assumptions: Students are selected uniformly; “without replacement” means the first student is removed before the second draw.

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must apply the given first-boy result and no-replacement condition to update both the boy count and class size.

items.answer_cues: Each distractor preserves one or both pre-draw counts, so the correct option is not singled out by style.

choice_pairs.assessment: A updates only the boy count; B updates only the class size.
A updates boys but not total; C updates neither count.
A retains total 25; D updates it to 24.
B updates total but not boys; C updates neither count.
B retains 10 boys; D updates it to 9.
C uses both original counts; D uses both post-draw counts.

items.answer_justification: Mean prize is ($1 + $4 + $6)/3 = $11/3; subtracting $3 gives $2/3, or about $0.67.
items.topic_fit: Expected net payoff with equally likely spinner outcomes and a fee.
items.assumptions: The three sectors are equal, so each payoff has probability 1/3; the fee is paid on every spin.

scenario_condition_use.assessment: The learner must average the three stated dollar outcomes and subtract the fee for a net result.

weak_distractors: B (-$0.33) and C ($1.33) do not follow clear omissions or arithmetic traps from the stated payoffs.
D ($1.00) could come from rounding the gross mean to $4 before subtracting the fee, but is a weak exact alternative.
items.answer_cues: A is the sole non-integer positive amount near the expected net; this is a modest cue alongside weak distractors.

choice_pairs.assessment: The results have opposite signs; B is not supported by the stated payoffs.

summary.overall_assessment: Five questions have supported keys. P02 is invalid because -$1.00 is absent. P02 and P06 strongly repeat the expected-net-gain decision and dollar-answer format. No complete item matches the three literal exclusion patterns; P03 is easy despite requiring counts before a complement can be taken. These author-only observations cannot establish worker qualification or repeated-bank reliability.
